title: Botany
summary: A plant is a set of solved problems: stand up without a skeleton, lift water without a pump, trade gas for water through a hole it can close. Read every structure as the answer to the problem it solves and most of this event becomes inference rather than recall.
objectives: Identify cell, tissue, root, stem, leaf and flower structures from a section or a specimen and state what each one does.
Trace water, sugar and mineral nutrients through a plant and name the force that moves each.
Place a plant in its group from vascular tissue, spores, seeds and flowers, and separate a monocot from a dicot.
Account for the light reactions, the Calvin cycle, and the C4 and CAM variants that dry climates favour.
Explain the plant's part in carbon, nitrogen and energy flow, and how plants compete within a community.
Diagnose a struggling plant from its symptoms, separating nutrient deficiency from infection.

units.title: Cells and Tissues
units.summary: Everything a plant can do traces back to three things an animal cell does not have: a wall, a large vacuole and plastids.
objectives: Name the structures that distinguish a plant cell and state what each contributes.
Classify a cell in a section as parenchyma, collenchyma or sclerenchyma and place its tissue in one of the three systems.

lessons.title: The Plant Cell
lessons.objective: Identify the cell wall, chloroplast, central vacuole and plasmodesmata in a micrograph and state the function of each.

lessons.title: Tissue Systems and Cell Types
lessons.objective: Assign a cell to parenchyma, collenchyma or sclerenchyma, and place a tissue in the dermal, ground or vascular system.

units.title: Roots, Stems and Leaves
units.summary: Three organs, one job each, and every anatomical detail in a section follows from the job.
objectives: Relate root, stem and leaf anatomy to absorption, support and photosynthesis.
Read a cross-section and name the tissue you are looking at.

lessons.title: Roots: Absorption and Anchorage
lessons.objective: Identify root hairs, cortex, endodermis and root cap in a root section, and explain what the Casparian strip controls.

lessons.title: Stems: Support, Transport and Storage
lessons.objective: Identify nodes, internodes, buds and vascular bundles on a stem, and name the modified stems that store food.

lessons.title: Leaves and the Stoma
lessons.objective: Identify cuticle, epidermis, palisade and spongy mesophyll and veins in a leaf section, and explain the trade-off a guard cell manages.

units.title: Growth and Differentiation
units.summary: A plant keeps unspecialised cells for life, which is why it can grow from its tips at any age and thicken for a century.
objectives: Distinguish primary from secondary growth and name the meristem responsible for each.
Predict a plant's response to light, gravity and touch from the hormone involved.

lessons.title: Meristems and Primary Growth
lessons.objective: Locate apical, lateral and intercalary meristems and explain how primary growth lengthens a root and a shoot.

lessons.title: Secondary Growth, Wood and Herbaceous Plants
lessons.objective: Explain how vascular and cork cambium add girth, and identify heartwood, sapwood and growth rings in a wood section.

lessons.title: Hormones and Tropisms
lessons.objective: Name the hormone behind phototropism, gravitropism and apical dominance, and predict which way a shoot bends.

units.title: Moving Water and Sugar
units.summary: Two transport tissues with two entirely different mechanisms, and the distinction between them is what this event reaches for most.
objectives: Contrast xylem and phloem in cell type, contents, direction and driving force.
State what raises and lowers the rate of transpiration.

lessons.title: Xylem and the Transpiration Stream
lessons.objective: Explain how cohesion, adhesion and tension lift water to a canopy without the plant spending energy, and list what changes the rate.

lessons.title: Phloem and Translocation
lessons.objective: Explain pressure flow from source to sink and say why phloem needs living cells when xylem does not.

units.title: Reproduction
units.summary: Every plant alternates between a spore-making generation and a gamete-making one, and which of the two you are looking at is the first question to settle.
objectives: Trace a life cycle through sporophyte and gametophyte and say which dominates in each group.
Identify flower parts and follow a pollen grain through to a seed and a fruit.

lessons.title: Alternation of Generations and Spore-Forming Bodies
lessons.objective: Label the sporophyte and gametophyte stages of a life cycle and locate the sporangium that produces the spores.

lessons.title: Flower Structure
lessons.objective: Identify sepals, petals, stamens and carpels on a flower or a diagram and state which parts are fertile.

lessons.title: Pollination and Pollinators
lessons.objective: Match a flower to its pollination syndrome and contrast wind pollination with animal pollination.

lessons.title: Seeds, Fruit and Dispersal
lessons.objective: Name the parts of a seed, classify a fruit, and match a dispersal mechanism to the structure that achieves it.

units.title: Plant Diversity
units.summary: Given any plant, the group follows from four yes-or-no questions: vascular tissue, seeds, flowers, and one cotyledon or two.
objectives: Separate algae, bryophytes, ferns, gymnosperms and angiosperms by vascular tissue, seeds and flowers.
Distinguish a monocot from a dicot from root, stem, leaf and flower alike.

lessons.title: Algae, Mosses and Ferns
lessons.objective: Distinguish algae, bryophytes and ferns by vascular tissue, rhizoids and spore-bearing structures, and say what cryptogam means.

lessons.title: Gymnosperms and Flowering Plants
lessons.objective: Contrast a conifer's cones with a flower and state what the seed, and then the flower, added to a land plant.

lessons.title: Monocots, Dicots and How Plants Are Named
lessons.objective: Assign a specimen to monocot or dicot from cotyledon number, venation, vascular bundles and floral parts, and read a binomial name.

units.title: Plants in Time
units.summary: Plants have been on land for some 450 million years and botany has been a science for rather less; the event asks about both histories.
objectives: Order the major innovations in plant evolution and say what each made possible on land.
Name the figures and the practices that turned plant description into a science.

lessons.title: Paleobotany and the Move onto Land
lessons.objective: Order vascular tissue, seeds and flowers on a timeline and name the fossil evidence behind each step.

lessons.title: The History of Botany
lessons.objective: Trace plant study from Theophrastus and Dioscorides through the herbals to Linnaean naming and the herbarium.

units.title: Photosynthesis and Energy
units.summary: The reaction the whole event orbits: light captured in one compartment, carbon fixed in another, and two variants for plants that cannot afford to hold their stomata open.
objectives: State the location, inputs and outputs of the light reactions and of the Calvin cycle.
Explain why C4 and CAM exist and where each one pays off.

lessons.title: The Light-Dependent Reactions
lessons.objective: Follow an electron from water through the two photosystems to NADPH and say where the ATP comes from.

lessons.title: The Calvin Cycle, C4 and CAM
lessons.objective: Trace carbon from carbon dioxide to sugar through the Calvin cycle and explain how C4 and CAM sidestep photorespiration.

lessons.title: Respiration and Primary Production
lessons.objective: Contrast photosynthesis with cellular respiration and distinguish gross from net primary production.

units.title: Plants in Ecosystems
units.summary: A plant is a carbon pump, a nitrogen customer and a competitor for light, and each of those roles turns up as its own question.
objectives: Place plants in the carbon and nitrogen cycles and name the organisms that do the fixing.
Explain how plants compete, and how a community changes after a disturbance.

lessons.title: The Carbon and Nitrogen Cycles
lessons.objective: Trace carbon and nitrogen through fixation, uptake, decomposition and release, and say where each is stored.

lessons.title: Competition and Succession
lessons.objective: Explain how plants compete for light, water and nutrients, and order the stages of primary and secondary succession.

lessons.title: Deficiency or Infection?
lessons.objective: Separate a nutrient deficiency from a pathogen infection using where on the plant the symptom appears and what it looks like.

units.title: Plants, People and the Bench
units.summary: What people do with plants is worth real points, and so is whether you can work a microscope station without losing five minutes to focusing.
objectives: Apply Mendelian inheritance to a plant cross and describe how a crop trait is fixed or engineered.
Work a specimen, slide or data station and record what is actually observed.

lessons.title: Mendelian Inheritance and Plant Breeding
lessons.objective: Predict offspring ratios for a monohybrid cross with a Punnett square and describe how a breeder fixes a trait.

lessons.title: Crops, Modified Plants and Plant Products
lessons.objective: Explain what makes a crop genetically modified, and name the food, fibre and medicinal products that plants supply.

lessons.title: Microscopes, Slides and Specimen Stations
lessons.objective: Prepare and focus a wet mount, choose a magnification, and record an observation from a preserved specimen or a data table.
